speechtext:
I rise, Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege, which action I delayed until the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources had returned to the house from the recent dominion-provincial conference.
It is reported in the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of November 19, 1957, that the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, when speaking to a Conservative nominating convention in Moose Jaw and referring to the cash advance proposal, said:
C.C.F. members oppose the move as useless, although it was supported by farm organizations.
My question of privilege is based on this false statement. The minister must know full well that every member of the C.C.F. party, far from opposing the legislation, voted for it. On the other hand, six members of the Liberal party opposed the measure by voting against the cash advance proposal. The C.C.F. members in supporting the proposal made it quite clear, as have the farm organizations, that cash advances, as a welcome first step, will not solve the problem of the cost-price squeeze facing western farmers, but that further comprehensive legislation is required.
I noticed in the same paper the minister's complaint of inadequacy of news reports on western members, and it would appear to me that this inadequacy is not being resolved by the distortion of facts by the minister. I am sure the minister will want to take the first opportunity of correcting the statement he has made and of giving an apology to the members of this group who have been misrepresented.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
maintopic: DOMINION-PROVINCIAL CONFERENCE STATEMENT ON PROCEEDINGS BY PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a statement to make concerning the dominion-provincial conference, and also I should like to table for the information of the house two copies of the communique as well as several copies of the report of the proceedings in English. A French translation thereof will be available shortly. In tabling copies of the preliminary verbatim report of the public proceedings of the dominion-provincial conference, I should like to make clear that the verbatim reports tabled herewith are those furnished to the conference immediately following the session, and have still to be corrected by the speakers themselves before they are issued in final, printed form, which will be distributed to each hon. member of the house in due course. The report speaks for itself in detail, and all I will do is give a general summary of the substance of the agreed communique.
In my letters to the provincial premiers of September 16 and October 31, which have been printed as appendices to Hansard, I indicated to the provinces the nature and purpose of the conference that we proposed. I think the accounts of the proceedings indicate clearly that the conference in fact carried out these intentions.
As I made clear in my opening statement to the conference, it was convened in order to seek the ideas and proposals of the provincial governments and to explain the general views of the dominion government. This government did not place any rigid formulas
1556	HOUSE OF COMMONS
Inquiries of the Ministry before the meeting for approval, nor did it adopt any take it or leave it attitude. It endeavoured to learn the up to date views of the provincial representatives.
I will not endeavour to recapitulate here the points of substance I made in my opening statement to the conference. Printed copies of that statement will be in the hands of hon. members in due course.
The agreed communique of the conference indicates that sufficient progress was made on certain items to permit action to be taken on them. In particular, the government is proposing to bring before parliament at this session an amendment to the Unemployment Assistance Act to remove the so-called threshold provision, under which the dominion treasury makes no contribution toward the cost of the eligible cases upon relief roles until they exceed .45 per cent of the provincial population. A suitable measure will be drafted and placed before the house in due course to carry out this policy, which should make it easier for a number of the provinces to make suitable arrangements to assist their municipalities in carrying this burden of assistance to persons in need. It is proposed to make this change effective at the beginning of 1958.
In my statement to the conference I said that the present government was inclined to recommend to parliament a change in the Hospital Insurance and Diagnostic Services Act to remove the clause providing that the payments to provinces under that act shall commence only when six provinces, containing at least half the population of Canada, have entered into agreements under it and have their own related acts in force. In place of that we would substitute a more definite date for commencement of the plan.
We found no provinces expressing any strong views against this change, and consequently I would now like to announce our intention of proceeding with it when opportunity offers. Consideration will have to be given as to what particular time will be selected and as to whether other changes in the legislation will be desirable.
I am sure all members of the house will welcome the announcement in the communique that:
It was generally agreed that the over-all economic position of the Atlantic provinces is now such as to justify some special grants in aid to the governments of those provinces from the federal government.
This is the most important immediate result of our meeting this week. The dominion government will now proceed to consider in detail what it should propose in order to implement this general policy.

The conference was invited to review the present tax sharing arrangements, and possible changes suggested by some of the provinces in the tax sharing arrangements act were discussed. As I made clear in my opening statement, the dominion government did not put forward any suggestions in this field, and it was understood that no endeavour would be made to reach definite conclusions on it at the meeting this week. Further consideration will be given by the government to this general subject in the light of the statements made during the public sessions by the provincial premiers, and also the subsequent discussion that took place in committee.
The discussions were generally held in a harmonious spirit, and I would like to pay my tribute personally at this time to the manner in which the provincial representatives came to the meeting to discuss in a most constructive manner questions of interest to all the provinces and to the nation as a whole. At the conclusion of the meeting the representatives of the provinces expressed their satisfaction at being able to put their views before the conference, both in open session and in committee. A subsequent meeting as soon as possible in the new year will be held in accordance with the proposals made by this government in calling the conference.

subtopic: CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY
CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext: Are the waters of the Arctic ocean north of the Arctic archipelago up to the north pole, in the so-called Canadian sector, Canadian waters?

speakeroldname: Hon. Alvin Hamilion (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: CANADIAN SOVEREIGNTY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the answer is that all the islands north of the mainland of Canada which comprise the Canadian Arctic archipelago are of course part of Canada. North of the limits of the archipelago, however, the position is complicated by unusual physical features. The Arctic ocean is covered for the most part of the year with polar pack ice having an average thickness of about eight feet. Leads of water do open up as a result of the pack ice being in continuous motion, but for practical purposes it might be said for the most part to be a permanently frozen sea. It will be seen, then, that the Arctic ocean north of the archipelago is not open water nor has it the stable qualities of land. Consequently the ordinary rules of international law may or may not have application.
Before making any decision regarding the status which Canada might wish to contend for this area, the government will consider every aspect of the question with due regard to the best interests of Canada and to international law.

speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to increase the length of seasonal benefit periods; to increase

Unemployment Insurance Act the number of benefit payments for which claimants may qualify during those periods; and to provide for other related matters.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Courtemanche in the chair.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SEASONAL BENEFIT PERIODS, PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish at the outset to thank the other parties in this house for their kind consent to allow me to proceed with the bill immediately following the debate on the resolution. I hope I will experience the wholehearted co-operation of hon. members in facilitating the passage of this bill. It must go through the Senate, pass the other house and receive royal assent. I am concerned that those who will be eligible for seasonal benefits under this new amendment will not be delayed in receiving those benefits.
During the past few weeks several hon. members have asked whether or not this government intends to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act this session. I think these questions were a reflection of the concern we all feel about the present situation with regard to employment.
Before explaining this bill, which proposes to amend the seasonal benefit provisions of the act, I should like to describe the present situation in what I believe to be its true perspective. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that the last period during which the state of employment gave rise to serious misgiving was the winter of 1954-55.
I should like you to look at the figures for two of the months that led up to that time, and compare them with the same two months in this year. We find that in August, 1954, those without jobs and seeking work comprised 3.1 per cent of the labour force. In August, 1957, those without jobs and seeking work comprised only 2.8 per cent of the labour force. In September, 1954, those without jobs and seeking work again amounted to 3.1 per cent of the labour force, while in September, 1957, those without jobs and seeking work were 3.2 per cent of the labour force. We come to October and we find that in 1954 those without jobs and seeking work were 3.3 per cent of the labour force, while in 1957 those without jobs and seeking work were 3.5 per cent of the labour force.
I think, Mr. Chairman, it is also important to note that the number of persons gainfully employed in this country increased by almost half a million between October, 1954 and October 1957, while the number without work increased by only about 28,000 in that same period. In view of these figures, Mr. Chairman, and without attempting to minimize our problems, I think it is fair to say that we have already come through situations that were
potentially as difficult as is the present one. Furthermore, a favourable factor now is that this government has no intention of sitting back and letting matters run their course.
Earlier in this session I noted that by curtailing the influx of immigrants for the balance of the year, by channelling $150 million into our economy for the construction of houses, by accenting the job finding activities of our national employment service, and by stepping up our winter employment campaign activities, we indicated our preoccupation with this problem. We are proposing now to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to increase the amount of benefit available to insured persons who are unemployed during the winter season when employment is most difficult to obtain. We estimate that the changes we propose would result in close to an additional $13 million of purchasing power being paid out to those who need it most and who can spend it to the best advantage.
At present the act provides that seasonal benefits may be paid for the period from the week in which January 1 falls to the week in which April 15 falls; that is, for sixteen weeks. However, even before January 1 there are substantial numbers of persons unemployed and unable to qualify for regular benefits, and also many are still unemployed when the present seasonal benefit period ends on April 15. The intent of this bill is to lengthen the seasonal benefit period by one month at each end, so that it will run from December 1 until May 15, that is for a period of 24 weeks. The effect that this lengthening of the seasonal benefit period will have can, perhaps, be best explained by reference to several basic examples.
First of all, there are two ways in which claimants may qualify for seasonal benefits. The first applies to those who do not have enough contributions to qualify for regular benefit but who, nevertheless, have 15 contribution weeks since the end of the previous March. The second applies to those who have had a regular claim terminate since the previous May 15, even though they may not have made a single contribution in that time. Under the present act those qualifying in the first group have a minimum duration of 10 weeks and a maximum of 16 weeks. The proposed revision will give a minimum of 13 weeks and a maximum of 24 weeks.
In regard to those qualifying in the second group, Mr. Chairman, the duration of benefit under the present act is the same as that authorized on the last regular claim with a minimum of 12 weeks and an automatic maximum of 16 weeks because of the end of the

Unemployment Insurance Act
seasonal benefit period. Our proposed revision will leave the minimum unchanged but does, of course, increase the maximum duration to 24 weeks; that is, a 50 per cent increase.
The effective date of this proposed legislation is December 1, and by that I mean that this bill will apply to all claims made in respect of the forthcoming seasonal benefit period. There is a minor exception to this and that would be those in the second group, those who had a regular claim expire since April 15, 1957, who will be able to qualify for seasonal benefit this winter on that basis. In future years, the requirement will be that they must have had a regular claim expire since the previous May 15.
Another point is that the privilege a seasonal benefit claimant now has of serving his waiting period during December will not be extended. In other words, he will now be treated as an ordinary claimant and will have to serve his waiting period at the beginning of his seasonal benefit period. This will not, however, put claimants in any less favourable a position since the date at which they can begin to be paid is advanced by three weeks and the maximum period of entitlement is being substantially increased.
We estimate that a large number of Canadian workers will benefit from the provisions of this amendment. Last winter, some
214.000	persons established seasonal benefit claims. This year since our proposed legislation will increase the period by two months, we might expect that the number who qualify will be somewhat higher. It would seem safe to say that some 250,000 workers will benefit to the extent, as I noted earlier, of some $13 million.

I should like also to bring out the point that this amendment, as well as the revocation of the married women's regulation announced the other day, is bound to result in an increase in the number of persons registered for employment with national employment offices across the country. Therefore, when hon. members ask about national registrations they are bound 96698-100
to see that they are higher after these provisions go into effect in Canada. There will be more people registered and also they may be registered for a longer period of time. Under the new fishermen's regulations which come into effect on January 1, fishermen will come under the provisions of the Unemployment Insurance Act and as a result will be eligible for seasonal benefits which are being extended in the resolution presently under discussion. Under these new regulations fishermen will now be entitled to receive unemployment insurance payments after only 15 weekly contributions. Provision is also being made in the amendment to seasonal benefit regulations for benefits to be awarded to certain classes of claimants who have exhausted their regular benefits. A number of fishermen could conceivably come under this provision.
That is all I have to say at this moment, Mr. Chairman, in explanation of this resolution and the bill which will follow, but I would ask hon. members to facilitate the passing of this amendment as quickly as possible. I would be very glad to answer any questions that might be asked, providing I know the answers. I do not, of course, profess to know the Unemployment Insurance Act thoroughly, but will endeavour to obtain the answers as soon as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all I want to clear up any misunderstandings which might be prevalent in this house as a result of the suggestion of the hon. house leader that there had been an arrangement with the three opposition parties to have this bill cleared through the commons in the one day. I am sure it would not be possible to make such an undertaking but it was tentatively agreed that should the bill get past the resolution stage we would not require the hon. minister to take a second day in which to introduce the bill, the hon.

Unemployment Insurance Act minister, having been kind enough to provide a draft bill to some of the opposition members earlier.
The hon. house leader did say last night at the close of the sitting:
We are never quite sure how long the other place will take to debate any of these measures as they are quite jealous of their rights.
Well of course members of the commons are equally jealous of their rights, as has been demonstrated on many occasions by members of the present government, so that we want it clearly understood that should this measure reach the second stage today we will be happy to go along with it. However, we do not wish the debate to be curtailed in any way.
The Minister of Labour in his opening remarks has gone to some length in attempting to minimize the unemployment situation today, in quoting the percentage of unemployment in relation to the labour force back in 1954. Now for that and other reasons I feel we should be entitled to quite adequate consideration of the unemployment situation as it exists. The fact that we now have a fall season for six months of the year is an indication that there is a very serious unemployment problem.
We have an old saying where I come from, high in the mountains where they do get frost almost every month of the year, as follows:
Of course we have only two seasons, the first of July and winter.
Now I do not think we want to have it generally understood with respect to all of Canada that we have summer for six months and the frozen winter for the other six months, so we must realize that this is an emergency measure which has been brought forward, the government having fully realized such an emergency situation, despite the remarks of the Minister of Finance last evening and on television during his press conference and his other remarks of less recent date in Toronto, when he was endeavouring to prove that there is today no serious unemployment situation.
I just want for a few moments to point out what is in fact the situation across Canada today. In British Columbia the lumber industry has fallen off about 30 per cent, which means at the present time we have close to, if not more than, 30,000 unemployed in that industry alone. The base metal industry is certainly in the doldrums and many are being laid off from day to day. There is a disconcerting sign in my own riding. In the hungry thirties gold mining was a profitable undertaking and I now find that in


the old Wild Horse creek area, where people were making a living during the early thirties, we now have a resurrection of the gold mining industry. They are erecting sluices and so on. Now while I welcome a new industry, I hope this is not a forecast for the future in the mining industry. We want to see gold doing well but we hope it does not mean that we are entering a time of depression when the gold industry indeed does flourish.
In Kitimat we have had some 1700 people laid off. These are the figures that occur to me at the moment but we know from day to day many people are being laid off. In Alberta, the oil industry is in a serious state of depression and much of that condition, I think, is due to the policies of the present government in stifling the gas and oil industry and related industries.
In other prairie provinces there is widespread unemployment. In respect to Ontario, in September there were some 27,000 unemployed in Toronto alone. And just the other day there were 2,400 laid off by the Ford Motor Company. These are large blocks but there are many smaller groups being laid off daily.
There are rapid cut-backs in the province of Quebec and in the maritimes, we have
35,000	unemployed and the labour force in relation to the rest of the country is very small. Yet, the Secretary of State, speaking at a Conservative rally the other day said that since the Conservatives came in they have created many jobs.
I am afraid the largest number of jobs they have created are in the unemployment insurance commission offices. I have clippings here-up to 20 of them-from various newspapers containing statements of responsible people about the serious situation which has evolved this fall.

speechtext: There were a lot of statements made on June 10.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SEASONAL BENEFIT PERIODS, PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
There was a question raised today in the House of Commons with respect to trade in the West Indies. That trade has been cut off for a period of almost six months now and no real effort has been made to settle the Canadian National steamship's strike and if something is not done soon there will be no revival of that trade.
That means a lot of unemployment, and certainly the fact that the sailors themselves are going to be out of jobs will cause another 250 to be unemployed.
One source says there will be up to 750,000 unemployed this winter. These forecasts must be made on the basis of some statistics which

support the contention. What is the government doing to alleviate this situation? They are releasing more money, it is true, for home building in the middle of winter when it is unlikely more homes will be started, but the fact that we are releasing more money to enable labourers to build homes costing between $12,000 and $16,000 is not going to put a great deal of steam into the building program. Something more will have to be done, because the very high cost of homes at the present time is beyond the capacity of ordinary workmen to build if there is to be any hope of paying for them.
When the present government was in opposition they had many remedies to recommend with regard to housing. The Minister of Public Works was asked only today whether the government intended to lower the interest rate in conformity with the action being taken by the chartered banks. When the present government was in opposition they made many requests that the interest rates should be reduced, and the down payment reduced to 5 per cent or even less. We welcome what has been done with regard to releasing more money, but let us go further and come to grips with the situation.
Unemployment is due to the fact that we now have a surplus of goods. The shelves, apparently, are loaded. In this situation the government sent out purchasing agents. They sent 50 people to the United Kingdom to purchase more goods and piled those shelves even higher. We certainly want to do everything to increase trade with Great Britain, but it seems to me that when we are already selling more to Britain than we are purchasing the salesmen should be coming from the other side, attempting to show the people of Canada the articles which they believe are able to compete in our markets. The government's action looks to me, personally, as being salesmanship in reverse. We have stocks on the farms and in the factories but we have to go out and look for more stocks for the farms and the factories. It may be all well and good, but it occurs to me, as an individual, that we are attempting to carry election promises a litle further than is possible-putting on a bit of a show. While we hope this has the desired effect with respect to trade I personally doubt it will do as much as we have been led to believe it will.
There are large numbers of unemployed in southern Ontario even in the electrical industry, yet we have been told that an order has been placed already for $10 million worth of electrical equipment, generators and so on. That is all well and good. We certainly realize that if we are going to sell to Britain we must also buy from her,

As I have said before, it does show that the government appreciates the fact that there is a serious unemployment situation in Canada, and that they are taking some steps to assist those who will be unemployed for a long Period. The fact that it will be possible for those who are unemployed during the Christmas season to begin receiving their benefits during the first week in December is indeed helpful. I note that the provision extends to the middle of May, in which month, in some areas, there are some signs of spring, though this year, regrettably, there is every indication that there will still be a large number of people unemployed at that date.
The minister has not indicated whether the government is prepared to replenish this emergency fund if necessary from the consolidated revenue fund. I think, personally, in view of the fact that this is an emergency and the government has indicated that it is now prepared to grant greater assistance to the provinces by eradicating the so-called threshold section of the assistance act, that they should not expect to retrieve these

Unemployment Insurance Act moneys from the unemployment insurance fund which, of course, is accumulated from the contributions of the employers, the employees and the government.
I think that is all I have to say. We welcome the legislation and more particularly we welcome the fact that the government is realizing that there is a most serious situation and is now prepared to face up to it and not delude the public any longer.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING SEASONAL BENEFIT PERIODS, PAYMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish first of all to thank the Minister of Labour for his rather straightforward and informative introduction to the proposals the government has in mind. I believe the information he has given as we enter the discussion at the resolution stage is such that we can intelligently discuss this proposal and it may very well have the result of requiring less extended discussion when we come to the second reading stage of the bill. I do feel, however, that at the resolution stage it is important for us to consider some aspects of the situation out of which this proposal comes and see it in its proper perspective.
The Minister of Finance apparently has been declaiming with great vigour on television and other places that we have no emergency unemployment situation. On the other hand I note that various spokesmen for the Liberal party, including the speaker who just took his seat, have been declaiming also with great vigour that the unemployment picture is very black and that we do have an emergency situation in terms of unemployment. Percentage statistics of the present total working force as compared with those without jobs and seeking work have been bandied back and forth. I want to say that at the present time at least I do not intend to engage in that particular discussion pro or con because I believe I can fairly say that we in the C.C.F. group have always maintained that an emergency exists if any one citizen in this country is unemployed and that the total of figures is simply multiplication of individual emergencies which should be dealt with and should be the concern of the members of this house.
There is without question, as the hon. member for Kootenay East suggested, more unemployment in the province of British Columbia this year than there was last year and when one finds those figures broken down to areas with which one is personally familiar and realizes that many of the people whom one knows personally are at this time finding a problem in seeking employment then of course it strikes home very directly.
I just noticed a little news dispatch which comes from the national employment service office of the commission in the area of the

constituency where I make my home which points out that at the date of this dispatch there were 1,450 persons unemployed in the area as compared with 456 unemployed at the same time the year before. I would certainly suggest that this proposal which the Minister of Labour is now bringing forward is the very least that we should have expected from the government in the light of the current situation.
We cannot help but be reminded, particularly in view of the fact that the minister himself made reference to the situation that prevailed in the winter of 1954-55, that there is some similarity between the approach the present government is taking and the approach taken by the government of that day in the face of growing unemployment. Some of us recall that chapter one of the statutes of the 1955 session, which was assented to early in January 1955, was an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act for the purpose of bringing the seasonal or supplementary benefits as they were then called to the level of the regular benefit payments.
In its essence the present proposal is another emergency rush-job tampering with the Unemployment Insurance Act. Certainly this action will be welcomed by the persons who will be able to draw additional benefits as a result of it. However, I think it is important at this stage when we are being asked to rush this legislation through that we should realize that this is in a sense a tampering with the act, that the approach we are being asked to make in dealing with this question of the extension of seasonal benefits is not really the kind of approach which should be made to the matter of amending the Unemployment Insurance Act; that it is something to which hon. members of this house should be able to give careful and detailed consideration in the industrial relations committee.
The question as to whether or not this particular proposal is the most desirable one which the government could bring forward at this time is one that requires careful examination. I do not propose to attempt to do that at any great length this afternoon but I think I might make reference to the most recent proposals for the amendment of the act brought in by the Canadian Labour Congress in their memorandum to the government on October 21, 1957. On page 14 of their printed memorandum they suggest the extension of the seasonal benefit period to include the month of December. I take it that the government is perhaps going a little beyond that particular proposal in the measure it is bringing in; but I would like to draw the attention of the committee to the

recommendation concerning the amending of the act which is made on the previous page, page 13 of the memorandum in which the Canadian Labour Congress has this to say:
We remain concerned about section 45. Despite its amendment, the conditions affecting eligibility for benefit remain onerous. Many claimants genuinely in the labour market are unable to establish a claim and there is good reason to fear that the approaching seasonal unemployment will swell the numbers of unemployed workers who will be deprived of benefit because of this section. We believe that this matter is sufficiently urgent for immediate action.
As I understand it the proposal which the Minister of Labour is bringing before the committee at this time does not deal in any way with a change in the conditions affecting the question of eligibility for benefit. Section 45 of the Unemployment Insurance Act is of course the section which sets out the basic requirements for regular benefits but the terms of eligibilty in respect of those desiring seasonal benefits who have not had previous claims, as I understand it, will remain at 15 weekly contributions prior to the making of an application.
The minister will recall that yesterday my colleague the hon. member for Skeena raised a problem which some of the fishermen on the British Columbia coast are having because of the 15-week requirement in respect of their eligibility for unemployment insurance this coming winter, pointing out that one of the reasons they have not been able to have the 15 weeks of unemployment was because of closure regulations introduced by the federal Department of Fisheries and the international Pacific salmon commission which operates under authority granted by this parliament.
Situations such as these, which have been brought to the attention of hon. members, do lend weight to the contention of the Canadian Labour Congress that the onerous conditions of eligibility are something about which we must continue to have great concern. I well recall, and perhaps the present minister may recall, that when the Unemployment Insurance Act was being revised in 1955, the then member for Cape Breton South and the other C.C.F. members of the industrial relations committee emphasized very strongly the fact that we could not consider our unemployment insurance system to be complete until it was such that all Canadian workers who became unemployed through no fault of their own were eligible to draw benefits under the act. As I phrased it myself at that time, if they had paid one contribution or one premium into the insurance fund. However, we are still a long way from that, and this proposed amendment will not really deal with that aspect of the situation, although it will mean,
Unemployment Insurance Act of course, as the minister says, that several million dollars more will be paid out in benefits.
This, of course, does raise some question in my mind as to where the benefits are to come from, because many of us who have followed the situation in respect of the unemployment insurance fund necessarily must have some concern about the balance in the fund and the income and outgo with respect to it. In my discussions of or reporting upon unemployment insurance matters to groups of workers in my area I have emphasized the fact that the unemployment insurance fund is something which rightly has to be regarded as a trust fund belonging to the working people of Canada. I have emphasized that it is not in the ordinary sense of the term part of the finances of the government of Canada but that it is a trust fund set up to be administered by a commission in the interests of the working people of Canada and therefore any payments made from it must be made under the terms of that trust and with an understanding that that is the situation that exists.
The last annual report of the unemployment insurance commission for the year ended March 31, 1957, does give us a report, as we would expect, upon the state of the fund. On page 32 there is a graph which shows that over the period from 1953 to March 31, 1957, the balance in the fund amounted to something over $800 million and that it has risen once or twice to a figure approaching $900 million. It also shows that there was quite a drop in the winter of heavy seasonal unemployment, the winter of 1954-55, to which the minister referred in his remarks.
The report contains another table which shows the total annual revenue and expenditure from the fund. It shows that in the winter of 1954-55, or during that fiscal year, something over $40 million more was paid out of the fund than was paid into it and that in the subsequent years of 1955-56 and 1956-57, while the income of the fund was somewhat greater than the outgo, that was as a result of the investment of the funds and the income from the investment. The report shows that if it were not for the investment income, the fund, on the basis of the direct contributions made by employees, employers and the government, would have been going into the red in each of the last two fiscal years which generally have been regarded as periods of relatively low unemployment. Therefore, when a proposal is brought in at this time, and when there are signs that do point to a much higher level of unemployment during this particular season than we have had during the last year or two, this is something which

Unemployment Insurance Act should be considered by this house when we deal with a proposal to increase the benefits.
The minister suggested, I believe, that according to his estimate-which I assume can only be an estimate-this proposal would result in additional payments of some $13 million. I take it this amount will be in addition to the $30-odd million which it was estimated was paid out in seasonal benefits during the last fiscal year. Therefore, I think we have to face the fact, and ask the question, as to how these additional benefits are to be financed. There are no references in the resolution as to any change in respect of the manner in which the moneys are to go into the fund, or in respect of the source or the amount. That being so, unless something is done, I think we shall have to recognize it is highly probable that the fund will be depleted as a result of payments made out of it during the coming season. In addition, when the fund is depleted the income from the investments will decline. In effect, there will be a bit of a spiral of decreasing income created.
Therefore, I would suggest that the government should be prepared to state its intentions in this respect. I would agree that the $800 million to $900 million in the fund, which has sometimes been called a cushion, makes it quite possible financially, without serious risk to the fund, for us to agree to this amendment to increase benefits at this time. But I do believe that the government should be prepared to tell the house what its intentions are in respect of amendments to the act or otherwise so that the security of the fund will be maintained.
I myself am inclined to think that this might be the appropriate time to consider whether or not some fresh approaches to the question could not be taken, because this situation of seasonal unemployment, and unemployment which really is not seasonal in its nature, arises out of the actions to a large degree of some of the large corporate interests in this country.
The hon. member for Kootenay East mentioned the lay-off of 2,400 men down in the Windsor area in the automobile industry. He mentioned the lay-off at Kitimat in the province of British Columbia of some 1,700 workers. I would suggest that that particular lay-off in Kitimat is one of the most flagrant examples of the complete irresponsibility of the large corporate interests in this country that we have had in quite a while, and that if corporations like the aluminum corporation in Canada are going to create unemployment like that, just at the flick of the wrist because of some particular managerial whim,
(Mr. Barnett.]

then the time has come when they will have to be assessed for their responsibility in creating the unemployment situation. All too long the working people of this country have put up with the complete heartlessness and ruthlessness of large employing interests who shove men out in the middle of the winter without homes or places or jobs to which to go, without any thought of what their responsibility is not only to those people as individuals but to this country as a nation.
The basis of contribution into the unemployment insurance fund rests on a principle that has application in a number of fields, namely on equal contributions from employees and employers with a smaller contribution in this particular case from the consolidated revenue fund of Canada. When we see that so much of this current unemployment is being created by actions such as the one I have described at Kitimat, then the question is raised as to whether that principle of contribution into this fund should be maintained in the future or whether perhaps the time has not come when there should be written into this act some form of penalty levy on employers who act in that irresponsible fashion.
I think perhaps an example of that approach is to be found in the workmen's compensation legislation across this country wherein is embodied the principle that employers are assessed an amount sufficient to cover payments required because of the accident rate within their particular industry. Perhaps the time has come when we might consider some such approach as that in respect of contributions to the unemployment insurance fund, namely some penalties for those employers who will take on a large block of the Canadian working force and then, without any regard to the over-all national picture, suddenly dump them on to the employment market, as it is called.
That proposal is naturally something which would require some careful study. I think it would have to be devised in such a way that there was some flexibility in respect of the normal rise and fall of employment levels in certain industries. However, I think it is particularly applicable in a case such as the one I have mentioned in Kitimat in respect of a construction program. Either under the Unemployment Insurance Act or under some other form of legislative guarantee to be required by the federal Department of Labour, if an employer undertakes to start a project which requires the employing of, for instance, 1,000, 2,000, 3,000 or 5,000 workers, I think perhaps they should be required, when they undertake that project to give some reasonable guarantee of the continuity of that

employment for a certain specified period or some guarantee of sufficient notice of their intention to lay these people off.
From time to time we have had in the house considerable discussion about the question of a shelf of public works. I think someone asked the Minister of Public Works not long ago some question as to whether the present government has a shelf. I would suggest that if we are going to have in this country a shelf of needed public works which may be undertaken, any government, no matter what their political complexion might be, should require that they be given some advance notice by these large employers as to when there is going to be a period when such a shelf would be required. It is obvious that if from time to time we are going to undertake various public developments geared to the fluctuations of industrial activity, those things cannot suddenly be put into high gear overnight and that a certain planning period is required. I think that an approach along this line could have quite beneficial results in respect of the number of people who are going to be making applications for benefits under the act and in respect of ensuring that the level of the fund would be protected when employers took action that dumped large numbers of people into the list of the unemployed.
I think I have made it clear that I am not suggesting that I feel this is a question that must be settled before this legislation is passed. However, as I said earlier, I think this question as to what is going to happen to the fund as a result of the increased drain on it is one which the government should be prepared to answer; and I believe that the government should be prepared to give us some indication as to what are their intentions. Unless they do that, while we will naturally be glad of a move which will alleviate the distress and the worry in the minds of a good many of the workers of Canada at this particular juncture, nevertheless there will be some good cause for worry in our minds as to what the future of the unemployment insurance plan in Canada is going to be.

I think we in this house too often find ourselves-

I indicated I was pleased that the minister had introduced this bill. It is an indication that while the former Liberal government of this country had adopted this policy to do a particular thing, the adoption of the tight money policy to raise interest rates and so stop inflation did not bring about that result. Now, the government finds itself in the unfortunate position of having to deal with the unemployment situation. This indicates only one thing, namely that the economic system of this country has failed us miserably. We must, therefore, have a look at it.
The Social Credit members of this house frequently have requested the government to establish a committee to examine into the actions of the Bank of Canada in respect to the tight money policy. In this way we could establish the effect on our monetary control, upon our labour force and all the other factors which might be involved. When I first heard that this legislation was to be put before us, I wondered what had caused the government to change its mind. Certainly, the government had indicated it had no intention of introducing such legislation. The minister says, that is right. I would say this to the minister and to other hon. members in the house, particularly our

Conservative friends, that they are saying in effect that members of parliament should not mention unfortunate problems in this house because those problems might become worse. I would say, sir, whether or not we spoke about this problem would make no difference. I would say that the tight money policy of the Liberals resulted in only one thing, namely that the Conservatives inherited it and, of course, having inherited it they want now to accept responsibility only for the good things and take none of the blame for the bad things.
May I suggest to you, sir, that the pretence there was little unemployment in this country would reflect no credit on any legislator in this house. We are fully aware of the conditions and this ostrich-like attitude of failing to recognize the problem would benefit no one. We know there is a problem. We are told there is a problem. We receive communications from our constituents indicating they are unemployed and asking what we can do to assist them. We read editorials in the newspapers indicating that there is a grave unemployment problem in this country, and yet we are told we should ignore it. We are told we are spreaders of gloom if we mention the question in the house, which is the logical place to raise this question, because it is through that means something might be done about it.
I have a clipping from the Vancouver Province of November 20 which interests me very much because the Minister of Justice was in British Columbia at that time discussing the very important question of the unemployment that might occur at Britannia mines unless this government took some action to forestall it. I am sure that all hon. members, as well as the members from British Columbia, are happy to see the mine in operation, despite the fact there was some talk about November 19 of closing it. However, in this article the Minister of Justice blamed the unemployment problem on the former Liberal government's tight money policy. The article says the Conservatives have relaxed the tight money as the first step in coping with the unemployment situation. Well, I do not know how long it takes parliament to feel the effects of a change. Certainly I think we all recognize that if inflation was stopped by the tight money policy, it has taken six or eight months to feel the effect of that particular change.
Our Conservative friends tell us that inflation is stopped. The Minister of Finance indicated just the other day that this is so. But it has taken from the first day when Walter Harris, former minister of finance, brought in the tight money policy up to now -a period of well over 1| years-to

apparently stop inflation, if it is stopped, and I doubt that very much. Now, in a matter of weeks, we are told that because the tight money policy has become loose unemployment is stopped overnight. How ridiculous can we get? The article goes on to say, in quoting Mr. Fulton's remarks:
The prophecies of doom indulged in by our opponents are grossly exaggerated and are not in the best interests of this nation.
"Spreaders of gloom" the Prime Minister called us. "Spreaders of doom" we are now termed by the Minister of Justice. Is a man a spreader of doom if he sees the unemployment situation is worse now than it was at the same time last year? Is he a spreader of doom if he can point to statistics to prove that very point? Certainly not. Is the same man a spreader of gloom, or for that matter a spreader of doom, if he is advised by his constituents that there are certain men and women who are having to go on relief in his constituency because there is no unemployment insurance available to them and because they cannot get jobs? Are these same individuals spreaders of gloom or of doom if they find there are more individuals unemployed during one week than there are in the next? I would say to the government, Mr. Chairman, through you, that it is our responsibility to draw these things to the attention of the government if that government-as is apparently the case- has not realized that we have in fact a serious unemployment situation. I say this because we are told it is not serious and that we are spreading gloom. If the government is not aware of these circumstances and we do become aware of them, is it not our responsibility to let the government know where it has failed and to try to suggest some remedy?
This may be gloomy to the Conservatives, but we in the Social Credit group do see a way out. We believe in making financially possible that which is physically possible, and there is a lot of work to be done in this regard. We just need to use our imaginations and our brains in the operation of our financial institutions so that we can make these things financially possible.
Hon. members will undoubtedly remember that not too many weeks ago I spoke during the throne speech debate with respect to this very same question. At that time I drew to the attention of the house a particular clipping from the British Columbian in which it was indicated that there were some 4,500 new jobs created but that the jobless list was high. It went on to point out that there were 4,500 men and 1,300 women or a total of 5,800 persons unemployed and 96698-101

No, that is not the answer and those may not be true statements. Unemployment Insurance Act stores are held up, the garage man on the corner has a gun stuck in his ribs and he is told to hand over the cash. These things are not so apparent or so frequent in good times when we have a period of full employment. Not at all.
This matter was drawn to the attention of the former minister, not just the fact of unemployment alone but the problems which were going to result from the policies carried out by the former government. That government had pretty well lost the lumber markets for my province. We drew to its attention the various changes which were needed to make it possible to sell more lumber, but the members of that government were prone to laughing and scoffing it off and to saying, "Well, we just didn't know the answers". It was not prepared to bring the dollar down to its dollar value; it was not prepared to accept sterling, whether convertible or block, in exchange for goods and finally develop its use in a foreign land which might use that particular kind of currency.
It was not prepared to take this particular problem sufficiently into consideration or to make the study that was warranted at that time. The continuance of these financial policies will result in the continuation of the problems of unemployment we face today; they will be repeated year in and year out. The fiscal policies which we have adopted, and which are being followed today, are outmoded as we have said time and again in this group. Those fiscal policies have proven false. Orthodox Liberals may say they are right. The Conservatives may say they are wrong. Yet there is not an individual in those groups, either among Liberals or Conservatives, who could point out the difference between the two policies which are accepted by those parties.
We, the unorthodox group, say it is time parliament had control of this money, and that it should not be left in the hands of a few individuals to do with it as they saw fit. The C.C.F. party say; let us socialize oil wells, gas wells, forests, dams, everything but what is mine. This will create more jobs without overproduction. How socializing anything would create more jobs, I do not know, but possibly some day they will explain. What has brought about the present difficulties? Several factors have contributed. There is the loss of the apple market in British Columbia, a situation which is well-established today, when Lebanon is supplying Great Britain, a market we supplied in full in earlier days. I think it is up to us to


discover causes and effects and, having discovered the cause of unemployment, it is up to us to try to cure it.
Here is another item from this same newspaper of November 20. One could make speeches about what one sees in newspapers in a single day. Here we read:
Fifteen million pounds imported, but B.C. tomatoes left to rot.
That is from the Vancouver Province of November 20. And here is another item: "Italy enters Canadian cloth market". We must find the answer to these problems. Unemployment insurance is not the answer to how we are going to keep people at work.

These suggestions were included in the most recent issue of the Canadian Labour Magazine for November, 1957. I am pleased to see that the minister has incorporated some of these ideas into his new bill.
In conclusion may I just say that this legislation, despite what the minister said earlier this session, despite the fact that the Prime Minister said we were spreaders of gloom and that there was no serious unemployment, despite the fact that the Minister of Justice said we were spreaders of doom and that there was no serious unemployment, is an admission by this government that it has no answer to the problem of keeping the people of this country at work.
I know we will be told that the new government has not been given a chance to develop its plans. But if they are to take credit for what the tight money policy has achieved they must accept the blame for what it failed to achieve, and if it does not keep the people employed they must accept full responsibility for that as well. The economic system we have today offers no solution to our problem. I say that in present circumstances this legislation is a "must", and that in all probability it will need to be improved. I wish to compliment the minister again for having brought it in, and say that it is my intention to support it.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, by now the hon. Minister of Labour must be well aware of the unemployment situation as revealed by the dominion bureau of statistics. It has been reported both in the press and in this house.
As my riding is primarily industrial, I too feel it my duty to draw his attention to the rapid increase in the numbers of unemployed. For instance, in the Montreal area alone the increase is 14,000, according to figures released from the Montreal unemployment insurance commission to the Montreal Star, of November 22. In the country at large, as reported by the hon. Minister of Labour on November 21,	1957, there were 188,362
unemployed last year, as at November 8, 1956. As of November 7, 1957 the number stands at 327,388.
What has caused this sharp decline in employment and how does the hon. minister explain it? I refer to Hansard of October 16 this year. Here, in reply to a question put 96698-101J
Unemployment Insurance Act by the member for Burnaby-Coquitlam, the minister says, and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, we are aware that there will be seasonal unemployment this winter. We have stepped up our winter program to take care of winter unemployment. We have also advised our national employment service offices to step up their tempo in obtaining jobs for people as soon as they become unemployed. I might say also, on behalf of the government, that we have curtailed for the balance of the year the influx of immigrants which swelled our total labour population. In addition we have channelled $150 million into our economy for the construction of houses. These are the things the government has done so far in order to cope with unemployment this winter.
How can the rise in unemployment be attributed to the usual seasonal decline? It has doubled within the year. Furthermore the minister assured us that the national employment bureau has been requested to find work for these men and women. I do not understand this, sir. Does the bureau now await the minister's order before it does the task it was set up to do? If jobs had been available surely the bureau could have filled them among the registered unemployed.
As far as the $150 million for the construction of houses is concerned, I would like to read what the president of l'Association des detaillants de bois du Quebec has to say about that. I quote:
( Translation):
Mr. Paul A. Durivage, of Montreal, will preside over this two day congress that will deal with several matters pertaining to the building industry. Ways and means will be sought to spur construction. For some months lumber dealers have been particularly concerned over the drastic slump in house building and delegates to the congress are planning representations to the federal government asking for other funds in addition to the $150,000,000 already made available.
(Text):
Moreover, certainly none of those presently unemployed will be able to benefit from that if they had been planning to build. The applicant for such loans must be able to show an increase. Here and there, however, the construction workers may temporarily benefit.
Now, coming back to the cause of this problem of increasing unemployment I contend that uncertainty and fear resulting from the Mont Tremblant conference are powerful factors. Industry became uneasy, afraid of the free trade policy proposed, and started to reduce capital expansion. For example, the Aluminum Company of Canada has halted construction on two smelters at Kitimat with the subsequent lay-off of 1,000 men. I quote from an article which appeared in the Gazette on November 1 which says:
Aluminium Limited does not see much point in making a capital investment of $30 million creating productive capacity for which there will be no demand.

Unemployment Insurance Act
Slowdowns in the manufacturing of electrical appliances and clothing have also contributed to the increase in the numbers without work as have those in the Canadian textile industry. Not only is management becoming reluctant to take a chance on expansion it is also reducing stocks. But I venture to say that unemployment would not be so severe now if business and industry had the same sense of security that was given them by the Liberal administration. On several occasions since I have been in the house I spoke on the subject of employment especially on the employment of older workers. In my opinion there are three categories of unemployed. First, there are those who are out of work because of lay-offs. Second, there are those who are out of work because of age, that is those who are age 40 and over. Third, there are those forced to retire at the age of 65.
On April 17, 1951 I outlined in this house measures that I believed would help prevent discrimination in employment because of age. The present Minister of Labour will probably then ask, "Why was nothing done by the previous administration?" In reply to that question I would point out that it did seek the co-operation of management through its film "Date of Birth" but prejudice and pension schemes are not changed nor overcome easily. Today, against the background of ever-increasing unemployment, the matter is even more urgent. As I pointed out in January 1957, "It is the workers over 40 who suffer most when production methods change". It is this group which also suffers most during periods of unemployment but workers of all ages want security of employment.
According to a survey conducted by the institute of public opinion and reported in La Presse on November 20 this year, 87 per cent of those questioned preferred steady work to increased wages. That demand has resulted in some cases in what is known as the guaranteed annual wage. Together with the demand for steady work is the demand for opportunity to work. Again I say that this latter is more often denied to the man of 40 or older. Those aged 65 have no chance of competing in the labour market. In this connection I was glad to see that in its policy declarations and resolutions for 195758 the Canadian Chamber of Commerce referring to employment of older workers had this to say:
Population forecasts indicate that the proportion of older persons will be increasing. The problem of the older worker must be faced if we are constantly to raise our national product, not place an unfair burden on the employed population, and enable those older competent people who wish to do so to remain in productive and useful employment.

Studies have indicated that the older worker if properly placed can compare favourably in performance with other workers and can make a considerable contribution to the production of the country. Furthermore, the older worker group represents a reservoir of skill and experience that the country can ill afford to waste. The addition of older workers to our labour force would enlarge our productive capacity.
The chamber is of the view that Canadian employers should give full consideration to the desirability of employing older workers in suitable employment to the fullest extent practicable.
And notice especially its recommendation:
The chamber urges that Canadian employers recognize the skill and experience of older workers and give consideration to the suitable employment of this group to the fullest extent practicable.
Surely if the problem is now recognized by an influential national body such as the Canadian chamber of commerce it is time for government to take steps to solve it. Much information regarding this class of workers, their capacities and abilities can be obtained from a book called "The Golden Years" by Senator Desmond of New York State. The state of Massachusetts with its anti-discrimination board has almost abolished discrimination in employment practice. What that state has done, Canada can do.
I maintain that the government at this session should set up a committee to study the causes of the increase in unemployment, ways of checking unemployment and ways of preventing discrimination against both those aged 40-plus and those now automatically retired at age 65 without regard to their skills, health or efficiency. It is only after a study of these questions and the establishment of a vested pension plan such as I outlined in January 1957 that we shall be able to assure our older workers of employment and avert unemployment in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like first of all, to congratulate the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) on his proposed amendment to the Unemployment Insurance Act. The increased benefit period will unquestionably prove most helpful to many unemployed workers in Canada, and in the constituency of Beauce in particular.
Nevertheless, I am sorry to note that, while the bill which will follow upon this resolution is bound to relieve unemployment, large numbers of unemployed will not benefit from this legislation. Now it so happens that in my constituency at least, they are the very ones who most need help. I shall now attempt to prove this statement with facts and figures.

For the last few weeks, in my visits to my constituency, I have personally studied the situation of the workers and have had others do likewise, and I have thus obtained some valuable information. Of course, I have had a pretty good knowledge of the situation, acquired over the last few years because on several occasions since I have been a member of this house, I have explained the difficulties facing the workers of my constituency and more particularly bush-workers and small farmers.
According to figures provided by the employment office at St. Georges, in mid-November 1956, there were 796 unemployed looking for jobs. Those figures apply to the constituency of Beauce and to the workers in commerce and industry. This year, for the same period, 1,642 people were in the same situation. In other words this year twice as many unemployed are looking for work as there were last year. I must admit that, as far as that category of workers is concerned, the present resolution providing for an increase in the number of weeks during which benefits may be paid, will be most helpful. Most of these workers have accumulated enough contributions over the last year or two to be entitled to normal and supplementary benefits and this payment will certainly be greeted with a great deal of satisfaction by the workers themselves and their families.
However, there remains the case of the bushworkers. There are two types of bush-workers, those whose chief occupation is employment in the bush, and then farmers and farmers' sons whose main occupation is farming but who, every year, go to work in the lumber camps to supplement farm income. Now that extra income is an extremely important item, and has been very much so over the past two years since net farm revenue has fallen off considerably, in line with rising costs of production. Just take, for instance, the constant increase in the price of fertilizers, feed and farm implements. Workers in this latter group usually received seasonal benefits because of the contributions they had accumulated in the fall when they were working in the bush. This year, however, they could not find jobs in the bush, they could not accumulate the required contributions. Therefore, they will not qualify for supplementary benefits and the improvements brought by the amendment to the act will not help them in any way.
Now then, what will happen to the first group of these workers, those whose main and generally sole occupation is working in
Unemployment Insurance Act the bush? I should say at this point that the figures which I am going to quote are approximate ones which I have collected in the course of my personal investigation. They reveal a rather serious situation and I would be very glad indeed if official figures showed them to be wrong.
There are about 6,000 workers in this group, approximately half of them usually working in the United States, the other half working either in Quebec or in Ontario. Of the 3,000 working in the United States there were 2,500 at work in October 1956 and only 225 at work in October 1957. This means that, in the constituency of Beauce, 2,275 bushworkers who usually work in the United States are at the present time unemployed. And, what is more tragic still, as it has not yet been found possible to conclude an agreement on the exchange of benefits between Canada and the states of Maine and New Hampshire, those 2,275 bushworkers have not accumulated any contributions because they had practically no work in the summer and will therefore receive neither regular nor supplementary benefits. Consequently, the excellent measure which this resolution leads us to expect will do nothing to brighten up their dark situation.
I should like to add incidentally that in the constituencies bordering on the state of Maine, the constituencies of Beauce, Dorchester and the others, there are about 18,000 Canadian bushworkers who generally work in the United States and who, for the reason mentioned a few minutes ago, can never take advantage of the Canadian Unemployment Insurance Act. I have in the past made representations to the Canadian department of labour requesting some agreement with the state of Maine in particular, and I know that the government of that state refuses to consider the matter.
The minister of labour of the previous government had looked into the matter. The present minister also takes an interest in the matter and I congratulate him for it. I therefore take this opportunity to ask him to keep trying to get the labour department of the state of Maine to change its policy. It would possibly be a good idea to explain to the authorities there that, unless there is a change, they will end up by being short of Canadian bushworkers. In fact the number of such workers going to the United States-outside of unemployment periods-has been dwindling at the rate of about 500 a year. If in a year or two there was a sudden increase of opportunities for employment in the bush, -which is quite possible, and I do hope it happens soon,-Maine will certainly be out on a limb, as far as Canadian bushworkers are concerned.

Unemployment Insurance Act
Now let us look at the situation of the
3.000	bushworkers of Beauce who usually work here in Canada. In October, 1956 there were approximately 2,500 at work, as against
2.000	only in October, 1957. In this group then, last October, we noted a decrease of 500, in other words an increase of 500 in the number of unemployed.
Now then, for the past few weeks woodcutting has stopped in several large lumber camps. The camps have closed down and some companies which usually end their operations by early January or soon after will suspend those operations within eight or ten days. It means that, if we add the number of unemployed workers of each of the two groups mentioned, we have, at the present time, approximately 3,400 unemployed and that there will be between 4,200 and 4,500 of them by the 10th or the 15th of December, out of a total force of 6,000 bushworkers. And here again, as the great majority of them worked in Canada this summer and became unemployed recently or some time ago, they will not qualify for the regular or for the supplementary benefits since woodcutting operations were very much reduced this year and the number of available workers much greater. As a consequence, operations were of much smaller duration and these people could not have a sufficient number of stamps affixed in their books to make them eligible for the benefits.
It is therefore, I believe, a conservative estimate to say that if the present regulations under the act remain in force there will be, on January 1st, in the constituency of Beauce, from 3,800 to 4,000 unemployed bushworkers who will not receive any unemployment insurance benefit and will not be helped by the proposed amendments to the act. How could the act be amended so as to give assistance to this large number of unemployed who do not qualify for benefits because they have not been able to accumulate the necessary contributions? I venture to suggest that it could be achieved by reducing the number of required contributions. As of now, the act requires 15 weekly contributions. But if that number were reduced to 10 or even 8, I believe that about 40 per cent of the 4,000 unassisted unemployed could obtain their benefits and would particularly be able to take advantage of the generous amendments the government is now bringing in by increasing the supplementary benefit period. This is, I know, an extraordinary change; it should of course be only temporary, but drastic situations call for drastic remedies.
And yet, there will remain the group of those who went across the border-about 2,500 of them-who will find it quite impossible to take advantage of the unemployment insurance act, even when amended as indicated by the government, and it would be so even if an amendment included my suggestion of cutting by half the number of contributions required to qualify for the benefits.
That group represents about 2,500 unemployed. Is it not a tragic situation? I confess to some reluctance in submitting a constructive suggestion in the case of this latter group. One way out would be to call for the enforcement of the Unemployment Assistance Act which authorizes the federal government to pay 50 per cent of the relief granted by the provinces to the unemployed and needy while the other half would be paid by the provinces themselves. This, however, brings back the sad memory of direct relief and the meagre allowance paid to idle human beings who could work and wished to do so. In my opinion, such a legislation should be but a last resort. Moreover, I understand that the province of Quebec has rejected that proposal and has refused to come to an understanding with the central government on that matter.
On the whole, would it not be preferable for the government to consider the possibility of undertaking certain projects, whose importance is shown by the persistence with which people in Canada have called for them for many years in certain areas, as, for example, the construction of retaining walls along the Chaudiere river in some parishes and villages of the county of Beauce? I know that in normal times, such projects should be carried out in accordance with the Water Conservation Assistance Act. However, we are in an unusual situation as far as employment is concerned and, for that very reason, the central government could carry out these works without encroaching upon the autonomy of the province of Quebec since they have recognized their responsibility in the matter of unemployment when they established unemployment insurance. Similarly, the government could also speed up the development of certain projects whose necessity they seem to have recognized since they are making plans for their implementation. Among these, I would mention the construction of a government building at St. Georges de Beauce. Such works, and many others as well, would stimulate the economy of the whole area and would greatly reduce unemployment.

I wish to be fair, however, and to recognize that the government is not unconcerned over the situation which now exists all over the country. The resolution dealing with a supplementary expenditure of $150 million for housing, which is now on the order paper, is ample proof of this and I warmly congratulate the government about this initia*-tive. However, I greatly fear that this excellent piece of legislation will bring no improvement to the particular situation existing at the present time in the county of Beauce, a situation which will surely worsen within a few months.
I have tried to explain very simply that situation as I see it and to offer my humble suggestions for its solution. I have the right to expect that the government, through its experts and even through the Minister of Labour, will be kind enough to give it their serious consideration. If they feel that my suggestions are impractical, I shall be glad and anxious, together with the population of Beauce county, to hear about better solutions.
