speechtext:
We are today giving consideration to resolution No. 13 which reads as follows:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act to increase the length of seasonal benefit periods; to increase the number of benefit payments for which claimants may qualify during those periods;-
That is basically what is being asked for under the resolution. It would seem that the intention of this resolution is to liberalize the periods and also the payments. I was a little bit concerned with regard to this particular resolution when I heard that fishermen are able to qualify under the act whereas, as I understand it, agricultural workers are still in the category of an excepted employment. In my own Okanagan Boundary area agriculture is our main industry. In that area are a great many workers who are engaged in agricultural work and pursuits. It would seem to me that it is only fair and reasonable that those agricultural workers be included under the act. Later on I should like the Minister of Labour to tell the house whether consideration was given to the matter of including agricultural workers under this scheme; and if not, why not? The very fact that fishermen are included and other occupations, such as agricultural workers, are not included I think is unfair and this act should be extended as soon as possible to cover other occupations.
Unemployment Insurance Act
However, there is one good feature of this proposal and that is there will be an additional sum of $13 million which will help to increase the purchasing power and the extent of the coverage will be increased by about 36,000 persons. However, I do feel that in so far as these amendments are concerned they are actually only in the nature of emergency legislation. They are only a palliative and not a remedy; that is one particular point I wish to mention. This is not a solution of the basic unemployment problem which we have in our country.
You are no doubt aware that in our country today there are two destroyers of progress: One is unemployment and the other is a lack of purchasing power. In my own Okanagan Boundary constituency we have a number of industries such as ranching, lumbering, base metal industries and fruitgrowing. Those persons who are engaged in those industries are having an exceedingly difficult time today. In my constituency unemployment has doubled and the situation is getting worse all the time.
In so far as British Columbia is concerned, information available from reports of local offices of the unemployment insurance commission pertains to the Pacific region, which comprises the Yukon Territory and all but the northeastern portion of the province, and as at September 19, 1957, the number of persons registered for employment at local offices in the Pacific region was 29,837. The figure for the comparable date, September 20, 1956, was 15,619. I would not doubt but that the figure has substantially increased since September 19, 1957. It is well known throughout this country that unemployed people congregate in British Columbia during the winter months and more particularly on the Pacific coast.
It is necessary that action be taken to combat this serious unemployment problem. I have not as yet received from the government any satisfactory answers to questions which I have asked. For example, under date of November 13, I put the following questions on the order paper:
What steps have been taken by the government since June 10th, 1957, to help the base metal mining industry in British Columbia and in particular the base metal mining industry in the Okanagan Boundary area?
What steps have been taken by the government since June 10th,	1957, to help the lumbering
industry in the province of British Columbia, and especially the small loggers who face adverse market conditions?
I should like to point out to the committee that since November 13 I have asked other questions pertaining to various matters about which we are concerned, and I have received answers to those questions. However, I have

Unemployment Insurance Act received no answer to this particular problem as yet, and it does relate to the matter oi unemployment. I am aware that this government did set up the sum of $150 million to help house construction, but it seems to me that British Columbia is being sadly neglected by this government. Apart from the matter of housing, I should like the government to tell us what has been done in so far as the construction of capital projects is concerned in British Columbia. I am not aware of any at the present time, except perhaps the expenditure of a certain amount of money in regard to housing.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, prior to the recess I was speaking on the Unemployment Insurance Act and unemployment generally. To me it is hard to realize that we in Canada have the unemployment situation which we do have, being aware as we are of Canada's rich heritage and its population of only about 16 million people. Yet we have a national debt of about $11 billion and our debt charges annually amount to about $500 million. This situation is indeed difficult to understand and it appears to me that it is a sad commentary on the performance of the previous and the past governments of this country.
I note at page 1360 of Hansard for November 21, 1957, the hon. member for Levis asked the Minister of Public Works this question:
Can he tell the house whether it is the intention of the government to launch now a special program of public works across Canada to alleviate the very serious unemployment situation?
In reply the hon. Minister of Public Works
said:
Well, I have no intention of launching an overall program of public works across Canada-
I think it is a most unfortunate state of affairs if that is the present policy of the Conservative government. It seems to me that this is indeed a defeatist attitude. What I am particularly concerned about is what the government plans to do to bring about a public works program across Canada and, in particular, to help the province of British Columbia. As I have said previously, apart from the matter of housing, I am not aware of any large capital project under construction in British Columbia at the present time. In my own constituency in the Okanagan Boundary area there is great difficulty in selling lumber at a reasonable price and the small holders are having great difficulty,

especially with respect to selling their fruit. As a matter of fact this year I have noticed many many tons of fruit have been dumped in various dumping grounds throughout the Okanagan Boundary area.
I am interested to know if when the yarious provincial premiers were here this week this matter was given consideration by them particularly with respect to a public works program for Canada. So far I have heard nothing whatsoever in this connection.
Now the Unemployment Insurance Act is no solution to the problem which is facing us in this country; it will certainly not give work to the people of Canada and unless something is done in this connection it will be the people of Canada who will be the sufferers.
I would like now to deal with that other destroyer of progress; I mentioned unemployment as one, and the second I consider to be the lack of sufficient purchasing power in the hands of the Canadian people. I say that if unemployment and the lack of purchasing power continues it could wreck the Conservative party. It could also be a sad blow to the welfare of our people. I am not thinking of the Conservative party, I am thinking of the Canadian people as a whole. I think there is one very important economic truth which we should remember which is that the sole purpose of production is consumption. This was said by the famous economist Adam Smith many many years ago and his statement is as true today in our country.
As we know production is no problem whatsoever; we have no problem in that regard in Canada at all, but the real problem faced by all parties in this country in years past and today is the problem of bringing about proper distribution of goods and services among the people; this is of course the problem of consumption. I know of nothing that is being done today to try to solve that particular problem.
I submit that our monetary system is old fashioned, it is archaic. As a matter of fact it is full of moth-holes and is in need of a new cloak. I would like to read a few remarks quoted in a newspaper entitled The Fundy Fisherman published at Black's Harbour, Charlotte county, New Brunswick. This particular issue was published on Wednesday, October 9, 1957, and the heading of the article is as follows:
Royal commission on finances needed. High interest, tight money condemned.
Another heading reads:
Bank of Canada methods challenged as unsuited to needs of present day.
The article reads as follows:
Premier Hugh John Flemming of New Brunswick has thrown his influence strongly behind the

rising tide of progress against the antiquated policies of the Bank of Canada. The premier, in a strongly worded speech before the Atlantic provinces' economic council called for a royal commission inquiry into the application of the Bank of Canada policies to the Canadian economy of the present day.
Now, Premier Flemming is actually a Conservative premier in the province of New Brunswick and personally I think he would be a welcome addition to the present Conservative party in this house. At least he would introduce into its ranks some flexible and constructive thought. The article goes on to say:
The New Brunswick leader's statement came at a time when evidence mounted daily to show the failure of the high interest, tight money to provide Canadians with increased production at a steady cost of living.
Further in the article it says:
In the United States, the rather odd monetary and economic situation we appear to be in, has resulted in the United States senate finance committee holding hearings on "the financial condition of the United States". These hearings began on June 18 and continued in high gear during July and August. The whole banking and financial structure of the United States is being subjected to a most careful and searching scrutiny.
I think that something similar should be under way in Canada. After all, our monetary system has not been given a really careful examination since the royal commission on banking and currency was appointed in 1933-almost a quarter of a century ago. The result of this royal commission was, of course, the setting up of the Bank of Canada.
Further on in the article Premier Flemming says this:
Is our present monetary and financial structure really suited to the needs of the Canadian economy in the mid-twentieth century? Is it too centralized? Can it not be made more flexible so as to meet, to some degree, the needs of particular regions? I think that these matters should be the subject of enquiry by a royal commission. We, in this region, are determined that the future shall be better than the past-that is the reason that we, the premiers of the Atlantic provinces, meet in conference here today. This is the purpose for which APEC exists. But all our efforts could be in vain if we are constantly faced with a monetary policy which is completely unsuited to our regional needs.
Now if they had this conference in the United States I submit that it is only reasonable that a similar inquiry should take place in our country. As I said in the first speech which I made in this house, it is high time that we had an independent group of men appointed to study all aspects of our financial system and to bring about a substantial improvement thereof for the benefit of the Canadian people as a whole. The Social Credit group, in making the amendment to the throne speech, recognized that it was time we had a scientific modern policy to bring an end to the tight money policy and to reduce the rise in cost of living.

speechtext:
I would like to start, Mr. Chairman, by saying a word of compliment to the minister for the very frank and concise statement he gave on this measure which is so important at this time. He is new to his job and his job is a difficult one. I think before this winter is over it will probably be the most difficult one in the cabinet of Canada. Nevertheless I think those of us on this side of the house, knowing the problems as we do, do congratulate the minister on the way he has faced up to and tried to give us the facts without evasion. I think his conduct might well be copied by one or two of his colleagues over there who have not been as frank in giving us the facts.
I am very glad of this chance to speak on this question of unemployment. I think that to many Canadians today this debate on unemployment is of much more immediate importance than the important debate on external affairs which took place yesterday. The minister gave a brief review of the conditions which necessitated the introduction of this emergency legislation and he also sketched in some of the things which this government had done in an attempt to solve the present serious unemployment conditions in this country.
Well, the Minister of Justice this afternoon, in another debate, said the proof of the pudding was in the eating, and I think perhaps the success of these measures mentioned by the minister can best be judged by their results. The results, as shown by the figures produced by the minister himself in recent weeks, are that unemployment in Canada is, on the whole, twice what it was this time last year, and the very fact that we are having to take special action today to hurry this legislation through, extending unemployment insurance benefits over a six-month period in the year, is also an indication of at least the appreciation of the Minister of Labour that this is an emergency. And all the brave words used by the Minister of Finance on the T.V. last night or in Toronto last week will not convince the Canadian people, especially the 327,000 registered unemployed as of November 7, that there is not an emergency in this country.
The fact that this legislation is going to extend what were seasonal benefits to cover half the working year is another striking example of the fact that we have a real problem in Canada today and the fact, too, that this legislation will extend to people who normally would have been covered by the present act but who have exhausted their benefits is further evidence.

Unemployment Insurance Act
I will not comment on the actions taken by the government to relieve unemployment, as listed by the minister, but I want to speak with special feeling about one action which the Conservative government has taken which, I am sure, is going to bring very serious consequences in my own province of British Columbia in particular as far as employment is concerned, and across Canada to a lesser degree. I say "to a lesser degree" because we in British Columbia are especially vulnerable in this field. When conditions are good in Canada they are very good in British Columbia; when things have been bad in Canada they have been very bad in British Columbia. We have greater swings in the economy, mainly because we are still, principally, producers of primary products. Today, in British Columbia, I see from studying the record, that we have a higher ratio of unemployment to population than any other province in Canada.
The government action I refer to is the announcement of the Prime Minister at a press conference at an airfield during the summer that he intended to try to divert 15 per cent of trade from the United States to the United Kingdom, a total volume of $625 million a year. We British Columbians find the biggest market for our three principal products the production of which is the chief source of employment in our province-in this American market, namely, our fish, our base metals and our lumber. I list them in growing order of importance, but in putting fish first I do so because it is the thing which is closest to my heart. We have been under considerable pressure, as far as our markets in the United States are concerned in recent years because of the cry of American protectionists groups to stop the flow of these products from our forests, seas and mountains into the United States.
I say that the action of the Canadian government in announcing that they intend to take $625 million worth of trade away from the United States has strengthened the hand of every protectionist in the United States who is clamouring for high tariffs against Canadian products.
I should like to deal briefly with each of the three main industries which, I contend, are likely to be adversely affected. First with regard to fisheries. We Canadians are blessed with tremendous fisheries, fisheries far greater than our population can make use of, and so we must look for foreign markets, and for foreign markets near at hand. Fish is not like wheat; it is not very storable, but highly perishable and the closest markets are best. Over one-half of our fish products today is sold for consumption and use in the United States.

In the last five years the New England senators and congressmen have maintained an important lobby to raise tariffs and bring in quotas against Canadian fish, and twice they have succeeded in having the tariff commission of the United States bring forward recommendations recommending tariffs which would have a most detrimental effect on the Canadian fishing industry. But we have good friends in the United States who value Canadian trade, and we have a good friend in President Eisenhower, because twice President Eisenhower has himself vetoed the recommendations of this tariff commission inspired by this protectionist lobby from the New England states. I say that President Eisenhower is going to have a more difficult time this spring in resisting the pressure for these tariffs from these New England senators, who can now say: "why should we worry about Canada, since Canada is devoted to taking $600 million of trade away from our markets."
An even more difficult situation prevails as far as our base metals are concerned. Canadian production in this field is far greater than a nation with a population of 16 million people can ever absorb. And, once again, the biggest and best market for base metal products is in the United States and, again, because prices have been sinking we have encountered a very powerful lobby mounted in Washington by the senators from the mining states of the west and by the miners union in the United States maintaining in senate representations last August that there should be introduced, not just tariffs but punitive tariffs on an extraordinary scale against the importation of our zinc and lead, a scale of tariffs increasing from one cent to two cents, three cents and four cents a pound on zinc and lead as they fall in price. Normally ad valorem tariffs increase, of course, as the price goes up but these tariffs will increase as the price goes down.
The whole purpose of these tariff recommendations was not to restrict the entry of Canadian zinc and lead but to block it completely. These hearings, which had been held over, are to resume this December. Earlier this week the Canadian mining association attended hearings in Washington to press the case of the Canadian mining industry, explaining the extent of its dependence on the American market and how, if these tariffs were brought in, at least one-third of our Canadian base metal mines would close immediately and the others be forced on to part-time production. There again is an example of how the action taken by this

government could have a dreadful effect on the industry of my province and, for that matter, on the base metal industry across Canada.
There is a third great industry in British Columbia based on our great timber production. Still in our province over 50 per cent of the payroll comes from our forests and here again the best market over the years for this tremendous production has been the United States, after which comes the Canadian market, and thirdly, and a long way behind, the British market. Once again we find these protectionist groups in the United States clamouring for tariffs against British Columbian lumber and, I expect, against maritime lumber, too. They have had a fair measure of success as far as plywoods and hardboards are concerned. Because of that, in my riding, in the riding of the hon. member for Comox-Alberni and in the riding of the hon. member for New Westminster, timber companies are closed or working with greatly reduced staffs with little opportunity for increased markets in the future. And once again those who are clamouring in the United States for still greater protection, as they call it-still greater exclusion really of our natural products are going to be greatly strengthened in their arguments in the senate and before the tariff commission. Once again they can say: "why should we worry about this Canadian government when as government policy they are trying to take $600 million worth of natural trade from us and divert it to the United Kingdom?"
The minister mentioned the impact of $150 million made available under national housing. That is a good step forward because housing probably does provide more labour per dollar spent than any other industry. The figures, however, show that in British Columbia there has been remarkably little advantage taken of those loans. Our province of British Columbia has generally led the nation in housing construction but the most recent figures on the distribution of that money show that while Ontario had taken $49 million, British Columbia had taken less than $3 million. That is about one-sixteenth of the amount, about one-quarter of the rate of construction in Ontario.
This matter of growing unemployment in British Columbia is one which has given great concern to all our British Columbian members. That is one reason why all British Columbia private members of all parties joined so unanimously in asking the government to take positive action in a case which we
Unemployment Insurance Act regard as a key case where very little government help can keep a great industry operating this winter. I refer, of course, to Britannia mines.
Now, it is true that unemployment insurance has changed the picture a bit so far as the plight of the unemployed is concerned. During the days of the Bennett government unemployment was the scourge of the people. The people were on the 20 cents a day dole and young men were herded into labour camps-out of sight out of mind-as apparently the Prime Minister would have us ignore unemployment today when he says we are creating a fear complex if we even mention it.
The floor of Liberal social security legislation brought in in the last 20 years, unemployment insurance, unemployment assistance paid jointly by the federal and provincial governments, universal old age pension and family allowances put cash money into the family group which did not exist of course during the thirties. All these things are helpful and the amendments put forward by the minister today are helpful but they are no substitute for employment. The answer to unemployment is not the diversion of trade from one country to another but the expansion of trade in every country and above all the development of secondary industry here in our own country. We want to see an expansion of jobs through national development. The government can take a great deal of immediate action to stimulate public works. Day after day we hear the Minister of Public Works say that these things are planned and are being revised or reviewed. This is not the time for the review of public works, this is the time for positive action and every possible public work contemplated should be undertaken as soon as possible.
There is one other item I would like to mention before I sit down. In his argument the minister pointed out how helpful the $13 million which he expected would be paid in these extra benefits would be as far as purchasing power is concerned and my Social Credit friend, the hon. member for New Westminster, concurred in that. I find that very curious economics. When they were working these men had at least three times that purchasing power, approximately $40 million; and to drop from $40 million when this group was working to $13 million when they are unemployed and drawing benefits does not seem to me to be very sensible economics.

In fact, Mr. Chairman, I have been rather impressed with the philosophy of the Conservative party which seems to be that unemployment is some sort of nervous disease that affects society, the sort of thing that attacks a hypochondriac, and that if you just pay no attention to his complaints they will go away, a sort of don't look now at the D.B.S. figures and perhaps the next time you look at their report unemployment will be gone. It is disturbing to me because I have lived long enough to have memories of previous governments which used to tell us that prosperity was just around the corner. It took us some 10 years to get around that corner.
I would also remind the hon. member for Coast-Capilano that while it is quite true that the Bennett government was apparently unable to do anything with the catastrophe that had overwhelmed the Canadian economy in 1929, there was the period from 1935 to 1939 when the Liberal government was equally helpless.

Now, Mr. Chairman, I think we have to take a more serious look at this situation and realize that it is not what the Prime Minister airily described the other day as a mere temporary situation. There are far too many serious portents on the horizon now to let us believe that this is something of a delusion, if we just avert our eyes from it.
I was interested in the suggestions from our friends of the Social Credit party that there was some magical way in which, by

Unemployment Insurance Act the manipulation of the monetary system, we were going to be able to overcome those problems. I was interested, too, to hear the hon. member for New Westminster demanding what was the socialist solution to the problem because you know, Mr. Chairman, I have been sitting here for five years and I have been disappointed session after session that I have never yet heard explained in this house just what is this miraculous method by which, by the manipulation of the monetary policy of the country, we are going to overcome serious economic dislocations.

Now, it seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that our friends of the Social Credit party are unable to distinguish between cause and effect, unable to distinguish between what is the moving force and what is the object that is moved in our society. They seem to have no grasp of the role which money plays in the modern economy, no grasp of the fact that as the former governor of the Bank of Canada told me in the banking and commerce committee in effect, it is nothing more than a reflection of the level of economic activity at a certain time.
I have been interested also in hearing from very many sources, including the extremely eminent Minister of Finance of Canada, talk -and backed up by our Social Credit friends -about the tight money policy of the previous Liberal government. Now, far be it from me to go to battle for the Liberal government, but I did notice during the election campaign that my Conservative and Social Credit opponents were violently attacking my Liberal opponent for the tight money policy of his government. My Liberal opponent was rash enough and ignorant enough to dash to the rescue of the government for the tight money policy that had existed.
I have referred before to those documents that we can get and I would refer hon. members who have ideas about tight money to look at the September report-it is the latest one I have-from the Bank of Canada and I think they will find the same situation even to a greater degree if they look at the


October issue. They will find that there is not a single month in the year 1957 in which the total money supply has not been larger than it was in the corresponding month of 1956.

My hon. friend asks me
about the interest rates. I have observed a strange sort of predilection on the part of the Minister of Finance to imagine, or at least to imply to us, that it has been some virtuous action on the part of himself and his colleagues which has caused the slight decline in interest rates which has taken place, the same line of reasoning which used to cause him to attack his predecessor in office and accuse him of having raised the interest rates. But, as anyone who has any grasp at all of the workings of the modern economy knows, he knows perfectly well that these interest rates were set by the demand for capital in a vast, booming period of expansion, and no action on the part of the government, either the former Liberal government or the Conservative government, had the slightest effect on those interest rates.
Sometimes we have pointed out to us the action of the Bank of Canada in altering discount rates and it seems that the governor of the Bank of Canada can speak until he is blue in the face and everything he utters falls on deaf ears when he tells us over and over again that the bank rate of the central bank of Canada is merely a reflection of the interest rates which have been achieved through the actions of our economy.
I would suggest to you, sir, that in this situation of unemployment that we are facing today we are not facing anything so simple as a mere manipulation of the monetary system; we are not facing anything so simple as some action-what action it would be I would not know-on the part of the Minister of Finance to lower or to raise interest rates. We are in effect reaching a position that it was practically inevitable we were going to reach, although for 20 years we have been able to avoid certain problems. But the problems come back again and they were outlined very ably just a few moments ago by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano. I may say I noted he also had the same sort of philosophy as our friends across the way when he suggested that the rash suggestion of the Prime Minister that he was going to divert 15 per cent of our trade to Great Britain had really caused a decline in our export markets. I do not think he really believes that. I think he knows enough about the workings of the international economy-

speechtext:
I understood the hon. member to mention the fact that our markets there had been curtailed and he linked that fact with the suggestion that it was caused by this rather rash and unconsidered statement of the Prime Minister. I think we are obliged to face the fact that no matter what we do or say those markets are going to shrink and are going to continue to shrink for some very simple reasons.
During those 20 years we have had a number of historical accidents which have enabled us to put off coping with this problem. We were bound to hit it now. We had, for instance, the period after the war when we had a tremendous backlog of demand and when also we had certain former rivals in the industrial field completely shattered as a result of the war. In the ensuing 20 years those countries have come back; they have rebuilt their economies and they have reproduced the situation in world trade that we faced 20 years ago.
There are various suggestions as to how we are going to cope with the resulting strains on our economy. I was interested the other day to get a copy of the text of a speech made by Mr. Graham Towers, the former governor of the Bank of Canada, to the life underwriters association in Toronto. It was delivered on November 14 of this year. At page 4 of that speech Mr. Towers is discussing inflation. I suspect that his comments are aimed at certain people who have been demanding that there shall be an end to the tight money policy and that there shall be a little more shot of inflation into our economy. He has this to say:
It should be noted that those who think continuing inflation is inevitable or even necessary do not regard it as a good thing, but rather as less evil than possible alternatives. One alternative which they have in mind is a situation in which demand is not pressing on supply, employment is less than full and credit policy not inflationary. Wage increases would of necessity have to be restrained, because increased costs could not be passed on to the consumer. It is assumed that in these circumstances, there would be a political swing to the left, particularly on the part of trade unions, and governments would be found willing to countenance and support inflation or perhaps turn to direct controls in an effort to combine full employment with some degree of stability in prices. So it is argued that it would be better to accept inflation-preferably creeping inflation-in the first place, rather than make an abortive attempt to avoid it.
Mr. Towers is, I suppose, the most eminent voice in Canada of orthodox capitalist finance.
I think it is of interest to us to realize what his view is on the now widely accepted theory
Unemployment Insurance Act of full employment as the goal of a worthwhile society. He has this to say:
In the course of this argument, we leave the field of economics and get into the field of human behaviour, because it is necessary to prophesy what the reaction of the majority will be to a given set of circumstances; and that is a very risky game, unless one goes to extremes in setting up the circumstances. For example, I think it would be quite safe to assume that massive and continuing unemployment on anything like the scale of the thirties, would produce formidable political reactions and adoption of policies of the kind I mentioned a moment ago. But can one assume that the same thing would occur if unemployment at times rose moderately above the average level of the post-war years? Government figures have put this at about 3.8 per cent of the working force in the United States and 3.1 per cent in Canada. The Canadian figure of course includes seasonal unemployment, which is much more of a factor in this country than it is in the United States. These unemployment figures have generally reflected a situation in which some unemployables are listed, plus others who are in the course of changing jobs and are out of work for only a brief period of time. Can unemployment go no higher than this without forcing the adoption of policies which impose on everyone the penalties of continuing inflation?
I have quoted that portion of the speech because it seems to me to reveal the fact that a very eminent spokesman for what is amusingly called the free enterprise economy considers that the theory of full employment is not a valid one and that in order to keep our economy working we must be prepared to have more than 3.1 per cent of our working force unemployed and run the risk of social and economic dislocation. I am interested in that suggestion because this afternoon the Minister of Labour quoted the figures for October of this year when he told us that 3.5 per cent of our working force was unemployed during October. The figure of 3.5 is considerably higher than the 3.1 figure mentioned by Mr. Towers. But, far from the people of Canada accepting 3.5% with equanimity, we have seen in this house this afternoon various members reporting from their constituencies the very serious plight of a large part of the working force of Canada. That leads me to the conclusion that those who speak in this vein-and may I say that it seems to me that those who speak in this vein are in essence supported by both the government party in this house and the official opposition and even more stridently by the Social Credit party-are prepared to have this type of unemployment as a means of keeping the economy going and putting the burden onto other people.
Some while ago I read the report of a speech made by one of the most eminent members in this chamber; I refer to the hon. member for Algoma East. It was a speech made shortly after the arrival of sputnik I on the horizon. During it he made this

Unemployment Insurance Act remark-and he will correct me if I have it incorrectly-or said something to this effect, that it now appears obvious that our social and economic organizations did not fit us to keep pace with the Russians. He qualified that statement later by saying that of course, even though it did not fit us to keep pace with the Russians, it was much to be preferred to that of the Russians and was much superior. It struck me, however, as a rather hopeful sign that a gentleman of his eminence should be prepared now in public to state that perhaps the time has come for a serious overhaul of our economic and social organization.

However, they have forgotten to say that a situation such as this does not spring overnight. If in certain parts of this country at this time there are a few areas where unemployment is prevalent, it can be attributed to the lack of foresight of the former government. It is from the former administration that we have inherited the situation facing us at this time.
However, it is of good omen that the Conservative party be called upon to deal with the situation. Every time this nation

has found itself in more or less difficult situations, it has turned to the Conservative party. I am happy to be a member of this party and to have the opportunity of helping my colleagues solve this problem which we inherited from our predecessors because of their lack of vision.
Workers in various centres will certainly be happy to learn that the benefits have been extended from 16 to 24 weeks under a Conservative government. In my own constituency of St. Hyacinthe-Bagot, official figures show that unemployment, far from increasing, has been decreasing.
Official figures which I obtained from the St. Hyacinthe unemployment insurance office show that last June there were about 1,500 unemployed registered at the local employment office. On October 31st last, always according to the figures from the unemployment insurance office in my district, this number was down to 1,100, which means a decrease of about 400 since we came to power in June last.
I would therefore like to draw the attention of this house and also of this country to the fact that the Conservative party is not the party of hunger, the party with a short memory or the party which spreads hardship everywhere but rather the party which can sympathize with human need, the party whose members all join here together trying to bring a solution to the problems left to us by our predecessors. In this, I choose to see evidence of the great satisfaction and also the great confidence we have in our Minister of Labour and in the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Diefenbaker).
I thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to take part in this debate for a few moments only in order to express my gratitude to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) with regard to the amendments he is bringing forward concerning the present Unemployment Insurance Act.
Like those who have taken part in this debate before me, I do wish however to express the fear that the suggested amendments may not be precisely those which we would have liked to be brought to this act, at least with regard to the area I represent in this house. On the few occasions when I have had the opportunity of speaking about this matter in this house, I have expressed the views of my constituents in this connection. I have asked, above all, for the decentralization of unemployment insurance offices and, then, for the simplification of the procedures to be complied with in order to obtain benefits.
I realize, Mr. Chairman, that when this proposed resolution has been adopted, the amendments will allow a certain number of people to receive benefits to which they would not have been entitled otherwise. According to the figures quoted by the minister, the number of people thus involved will range between 30,000 and 40,000.
I respectfully submit Mr. Chairman, that one of the amendments which had been forecast and which hon. members were expecting concerned the qualifications of claimants, a provision which will be found in section 50, subsection 2 of the legislation. The amendment I have in mind would have reduced at least from 15 to 10 the number of stamps required for qualification in the case of those who claim unemployment insurance benefits.
Like the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Poulin)-his constituency is nearly adjacent my own or, at least, has the same general living conditions-I will state that those who have been most seriously hit in previous years

by unemployment are in the first place workers in the construction industries and then bushworkers.
If it is recognized that there are unemployed people at this time in these two classes of workers, we also know that a great number of those workers have not worked long enough since March 31 to accumulate a sufficient number of stamps to make them eligible for the benefits and, consequently, they will not be helped by the improvements in the act, as they nevertheless might have hoped to be.
Another point on which I wish to draw your attention, Mr. Chairman, is the state of emergency which is invoked for the presentation of this bill. To my mind, it is somewhat contradictory to propose an amendment to the act presumably because of a state of urgency and not providing that this amendment is only for a temporary period.
According to information given us by the minister, the amendments to this act will cost the unemployment insurance fund at least 15 million dollars and most likely a still greater amount. It means that the present unemployment situation is not normal and that, as the case of the unemployed people is to be considered as a whole, the amendments must be helpful to the majority, whatever their effects on the fund, even if afterwards the fund has to be brought back to its present level.
A short while ago I heard the hon. member for St. Hyacinthe-Bagot (Mr. Ricard) say that the Conservative party was not the party of unemployment and hardship. Well, I say to him that if he wants to place the blame for unemployment on a political party, the Liberal party has many achievements to its credit. During 22 years, as was so well said by the former minister of fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) a few moments ago, the Liberal party, through the numerous social security measures which it has introduced, including this Unemployment Insurance Act which now serves as an expedient to the Conservative party to cope at least in part with the present serious situation, has not been a negative but a truly positive party. Without all the measures which have been introduced by the party to which I belong, I wonder in what situation the population of the whole of Canada would be at the present time.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it was with great interest that I listened this afternoon to the explanations given to the house with regard to this measure which I would call emergency legislation designed to relieve unemployment. I do not think that we should entertain any illusions about this for, in spite of the optimistic statements of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) unemployment is becoming a national danger and we have every reason to feel anxious about it.
Naturally enough, as this measure comes up for discussion, I feel I should recall briefly that in my first speech in this house on October 18 last I referred to this unemployment problem which is possibly more serious in my constituency of Dorchester than anywhere else in the Quebec area. At the time I had reminded hon. members of the fact that the working people who make up my constituency are, for the most part, farmers who because of the poor quality of the land, find it necessary to work several weeks a year in the forests of Quebec and often also in those of the United States.
The minister is not unaware of the fact that lumbering operations on the Canadian side of the border have been reduced. According to information at my disposal I believe I can state that it has been reduced in the proportion of 60 per cent. On the other hand certain American companies have even decided this year to close down operations entirely. All this has had in my constituency results which are not difficult to imagine, that is, increasing unemployment and great anxiety on the part of hundreds of heads of families on the approach of winter.
It is for those reasons that in the very first days of the session I respectfully submitted to the government the urgency of amending unemployment insurance legislation in order to relieve that unemployment. I had also suggested that these seasonal benefits be paid as of December 1 and I am happy to note that the department has lengthened the period provided by adding a month at the beginning and another month at the end. I know that that particular aspect of the legislation will be greatly appreciated in my constituency as well as in every other working constituency in Canada. Unfortunately, I regret that the minister did not see fit to accept my second suggestion which, in my humble opinion, was far more important than the one dealing with the extension of benefits.

I had in fact expressed the opinion that the government should lower from 15 to 10 the number of contributions required for qualification for the seasonal benefits and I notice with great disappointment for the unemployed of my constituency that this was not considered favourably. I regret that the government did not see fit to adopt this suggestion all the more so because I believe that a measure such as the one just proposed by the Minister of Labour misses the objective- completely in our case and partially elsewhere-which the minister no doubt had in mind.
The measure as proposed will not unfortunately have the good effects which a reduction of the required contributions would have had for my constituents because most of our unemployed, as a result of lack of work in the lumber camps, have been unable to accumulate enough contributions to qualify for seasonal benefits.
And we will have a rather sorry situation where a measure intended, in short, to assist the unemployed will precisely penalize those people for not having accumulated enough contributions.
I notice with pleasure in this proposal that the minister took into account the special situation of an important part of our population, namely the fishermen. Without knowing all the details of the measure, I believe it will be highly appreciated by this class of Canadian workers. However, I am still wondering why the Minister of Labour did not consider proposing an improvement in favour of our farmers by the repeal of the section of the Unemployment Insurance Act which requires them to pay 22 contributions or at least to prove that they worked outside the farm for at least 22 weeks in order to qualify for the seasonal benefits.
Allow me, Mr. Chairman, to suggest to the hon. minister to take in serious consideration these few remarks and to alleviate, as much as possible, the distress which is now felt in this country. I have welcomed the recent statement of the hon. minister about the changes made to the unemployment insurance regulations concerning married women. But this is not the most serious problem, in my view, and it would have been much more important to consider the case of the heads of family and of the farmers of our rural areas.
Naturally, Mr. Chairman, we all know that such a measure is but a temporary remedy. It will not settle at all the serious problem of unemployment, let alone relieve the government of its obligation to take the necessary steps to cope with unemployment. The Cana-
Unemployment Insurance Act dian worker will accept this expedient but would prefer a tonic which would restore his health.
I have received today a copy of a letter addressed to the hon. Minister of Labour by Mr. Philip E. Smyth, representative of an international organization. This letter was accompanied by a copy of an article published in a Washington newspaper and announcing that a conference between representatives of the United States and Canada would meet in Ottawa, on December 1st next, to study Canadian-American affairs, particularly from the economic point of view. May I express the wish that, in the course of that meeting, the hon. Minister of Labour will succeed in coming to an understanding with the authorities of the States of Maine and New Hampshire on the question of reciprocity in the matter of unemployment insurance so that our Canadian workers who must earn their living in the neighbouring country but who, nevertheless, are Canadian taxpayers, can benefit from our Unemployment Insurance Act when they come back home on account of a shortage of work. May these few suggestions convince the hon. Minister of Labour that we are following with much interest and anxiety, on behalf of our electors, any forward move that may be made to improve our Unemployment Insurance Act which, in view of the urgency of the present situation, is necessarily inadequate and ineffective in some areas as hard hit as my constituency.

speechtext:
I am very much in favour
of this resolution which provides for a bill enabling the government to make payment of seasonal unemployment benefits starting December 1 instead of January 1. I might say that I am sorry indeed that the government finds it necessary to have seasonal unemployment benefits extended. In the 1955 session I had a resolution on the order paper suggesting higher regular unemployment and supplementary benefit payments under the Unemployment Insurance Act. At that time my resolution was superseded by amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act introduced into this house by the government.
I may say that at that time there was considerable unemployment in my riding and I even came into the house and dared to use the word "unemployment". I might say that in speaking at the resolution stage of that bill I referred to unemployment several times and my repetitious use of that word

Unemployment Insurance Act [DOT]"unemployment" was exceeded only by those now sitting on the government side of the house. I might say that a week or two prior to that time the present Minister of Labour expounded at great length on unemployment and the perils of unemployment.
I think he was referring to Oshawa at that time.
At that time, as may be found in Hansard, I said that responsible heads of municipalities, heads of unions and others came to me complaining about the inadequacy of the Unemployment Insurance Act, which representation I brought here to parliament. These same heads of municipalities and these same heads of unions are coming to me now complaining that many of these unemployed workers cannot get any unemployment insurance benefits. They tell me now that unemployment will become worse as the winter progresses. I thought I heard the Minister of Labour say the other day that unemployment might even reach the halfmillion mark. I may be wrong in that figure but I have seen other references saying that unemployment might reach the figure of 750,000.
I maintain that unemployment insurance figures as announced in this house do not present a proper picture of the situation. In parts of my riding there are people who are working part time; they work two or three days a week and they are not classified as unemployed, but they have a hard time to meet their financial obligations. Our unemployed and those on short time have certain fixed obligations which they must meet. They must meet rent, heat, tax, insurance and public utility bills. These costs must be paid because they are fixed. Some have bought new homes and furniture on a monthly payment plan. In my part of the country foreclosures on mortgages and seizures by the bailiff of furniture and so on are beginning to appear. These actions certainly do not assure others who feel that they are approaching the same condition financially.
One aspect in this whole matter is that with all of them the family budget is tight and the amount that is left for food is much less than it used to be. I think we should see that our people, particularly our children, have adequate food-an adequate, nutritious diet-in order that they may have maximum health. At that time I argued against cutting off seasonal unemployment insurance benefits as of April 15. I thought at that time that we would have a considerable number of unemployed on that date, but employment conditions improved and by April 15 we did not have so many as had been predicted

here in the house. April 15 was close at hand and that is why on April 4 a good many members in this house argued for the extension until May 15. Likewise, at this time when unemployment is mounting, I am very much in favour of advancing this date to December 1 when supplementary payments may begin.
In Canada, because of our climate, we are bound to have considerable seasonal unemployment. I think, too, that in our free enterprise system-and in fact in almost any system-we are bound to have some ups and downs in unemployment. A good part of our economy depends on world trade. I therefore think our government should do very little to interfere with the free flow of trade. Our government has sent a very expensive trade mission to Great Britain. Its purpose is to purchase only, as announced by the high commissioner in London, and it was announced in this house that its purpose was chiefly to buy. I can assure you that the unemployed in my area are more interested in helping to make things that they can sell than in buying something that they cannot pay for.
The members of the government when in opposition always talked about processing our own raw materials. Not once since I have been here this session have I heard any member of the government say anything about the fabrication of our raw materials. The former leader of the Conservative party, Mr. Drew, two or three times every session, I believe, talked about the processing of our raw materials. Certainly he gave that as one of the ways in which to cure unemployment at the time of the debate we had in April, 1955.
I am in favour of doing all we can to trade with Great Britain but all the articles that I read in the papers say that there is little or no unemployment in that country. I was a little bit surprised when the leader of this buying trade commission to Great Britain placed a good will order of $10 million in that country for certain hydro materials, and this at a time when we have unemployment in Peterborough, Hamilton, Toronto and the Niagara district where hydro have placed orders for their requirements in the past. I should like to have from this government some assurance that when we in this country buy British manufactured articles and Britain earns Canadian dollars she will spend those dollars in the purchase of our wheat and of our other raw materials. When I say this I have in mind the fact that while the Minister of Trade and Commerce was in Britain this fall, wheat was bought from the United States but I understand that no wheat was bought here in Canada.
We live in a country rich in natural resources and I think that this government

is admitting defeat when they introduce this sort of legislation to look after unemployment. Surely, this is an indictment of the government that promised Canadians almost everything under the sun at election time. I think instead of having to extend this insurance measure, the government should find jobs for our people.

I am pleased to be able to congratulate the minister upon these benefits, and I shall be very brief on this subject. I just want to draw the attention of the minister to two complaints that have often been received from my district. The first is with reference to article 47 which fixes the weekly benefit for the unemployed on the basis of the average weekly contributions for the last 30 weeks. It often happens that some people who are employed on an hourly or day-to-day basis, and who earn more than $60 a week, suffer from the fact that during the last 30 weeks they have missed a few hours or a few days work and so their average is lower than it should be. It seems to me that in such cases the average should be based on more than 30 weeks, and perhaps the unemployment office could take into account the previous year, if there are enough stamps for that.
Another complaint I receive often arises from the fact that in our district some people are obliged to work for farmers. In those cases they are losing the benefit of the stamps. Would it not be possible to amend the law so as to enable people who desire to pay for their stamps to do so, even if the farmers themselves are not obliged to pay for stamps. There should be a system to enable these employees to pay for their stamps if they so desired, so that they would be entitled to the benefit of insurance.

National Health and Welfare):
Persons receiving allowances under the Disabled Persons Act numbered 35,540 as at September 30, 1957. Such persons had been medically certified as being totally and permanently disabled.
